title: Generating from Discrete Distributions Using Diffusions: Insights from Random Constraint Satisfaction Problems
claim: Learned denoisers match the ideal one, continuous diffusion beats discrete, and smart variable ordering further improves success near the phase transition.
layout: 2 panels side by side, shared y-axis, arrows annotating gaps, dashed vertical threshold line
description: Two line plots side by side, both with success rate (0 to 1) on the y-axis and clause density alpha on the x-axis, and a shared legend across the top. The left panel shows blue (continuous) and red (discrete) curves. Solid lines are the learned NN denoiser and dashed lines are the BP denoiser, with shaded confidence bands. The blue curves stay near 1 until about alpha=5 and then fall. The red curves fall much earlier. A tall black arrow labeled 'disc. → cont.' marks the gap between them. The right panel shows three red-to-dark-maroon curves for random, reverse-degree and dynamic reverse-degree ordering. The darker curves sit higher. A short arrow labeled 'smart ordering' marks the improvement. A purple dashed vertical line marks alpha_d, the dynamical phase transition, in both panels. The eye goes first to the blue/red separation and the arrow in the left panel.
caption: 4-SAT (N = 300) Left: The learned NN denoiser (solid) matches the BP denoiser (dashed), and continuous diffusion (blue) outperforms discrete diffusion (red) for both denoisers at locality radius r = 3. Right: Smart variable ordering improves discrete diffusion with r = 100 BP denoiser. We compare random ordering with reverse-degree and dynamic reverse-degree orderings. We report success rate (probability of producing a satisfying assignment) versus clause density α, averaged over 500 random formulas. Shaded regions: 95% confidence interval. Vertical line: dynamical phase transition αd(k = 4) ≈9.38.
abstract: Generating data from discrete distributions is important for a number of application domains including text, tabular data, and genomic data. Several groups have recently used random $k$-satisfiability ($k$-SAT) as a synthetic benchmark for new generative techniques. In this paper, we show that fundamental insights from the theory of random constraint satisfaction problems have observable implications (sometime contradicting intuition) on the behavior of generative techniques on such benchmarks. More precisely, we study the problem of generating a uniformly random solution of a given (random) $k$-SAT or $k$-XORSAT formula. Among other findings, we observe that: $(i)$~Continuous diffusions outperform masked discrete diffusions; $(ii)$~Learned diffusions can match the theoretical `ideal' accuracy; $(iii)$~Smart ordering of the variables can significantly improve accuracy, although not following popular heuristics.
